notes.meaning: Jesus shares a deep and unique relationship with God the Father that no human being can fully understand on their own. The Father has placed all authority and spiritual knowledge into the hands of the Son. People cannot come to know God through human wisdom alone, but only when Jesus chooses to reveal Him.

differ.view: Lutherans view this passage through the distinction between the hidden God and the revealed God, teaching that apart from Christ God is unknowable and frightening, but in Jesus He makes Himself known as a loving Savior.

notes.meaning: Jesus privately reminds His followers how blessed they are to see and hear His ministry firsthand. For centuries, faithful kings and Old Testament prophets longed to see the promised Savior, but they only caught glimpses from afar. The disciples are now witnessing the fulfillment of those ancient promises with their very own eyes.

An expert in the Jewish law stands up to test Jesus and see if His teaching agrees with scripture. He asks what deeds he must perform in order to inherit eternal life, meaning unending life in friendship with God. His question assumes that salvation is something a person earns by doing good works.

Jesus answers by directing the legal scholar back to the Scriptures he studied every day. Since the man's profession was explaining the law of Moses, Jesus asks him how he understands what God has written. This approach kindly challenges the lawyer to examine the true demands of God's word.

The lawyer recites the two greatest commands in scripture: to love God completely and to love your neighbor as yourself. Loving God means giving Him our entire heart, soul, strength, and mind. Showing care and kindness to other people flows directly out of this total devotion to God.

Jesus confirms that the lawyer gave the correct biblical answer. If someone could truly obey these two great commands without ever failing, that person would live. Jesus speaks this way to help the man see that no one can ever keep God's law perfectly on their own.

differ.view: Some evangelicals emphasize that Jesus was not teaching that people earn heaven through good works, but was using the law's impossible standard to convince the man that he needed God's mercy.

notes.meaning: The lawyer realizes he has fallen short, so he searches for an excuse to prove he is righteous. Religious teachers back then often taught that only fellow Jews counted as neighbors, leaving out foreigners and enemies. By asking who his neighbor is, he hopes to set an easy limit on whom he is required to love.

Jesus replies by telling a story about a traveler walking down the steep, rocky highway from Jerusalem to Jericho. Bandits ambush him, strip off his clothes, beat him severely, and leave him near death on the road. The wounded traveler is completely helpless and unable to rescue himself.

A Jewish priest happens to come down the same road and sees the battered traveler. Instead of stopping to assist him, the priest crosses to the other side of the road and keeps moving. Even though his sacred office was meant to show God's mercy, he turns his back on a dying countryman.

A Levite, who served as a helper in the temple worship, arrives at the spot next and looks at the injured man. Just like the priest, he crosses over to the far side of the road and walks away without helping. Both religious leaders choose their own comfort and safety over caring for a neighbor in crisis.

A traveler from Samaria comes along the road and catches sight of the dying stranger. Jews and Samaritans were bitter enemies who usually refused to have anything to do with each other. Yet when this foreigner sees the suffering man, he is moved with deep, heartfelt compassion.

The Samaritan goes straight to the man and bandages his injuries, pouring on wine to clean them and olive oil to soothe the pain. He places the wounded traveler on his own donkey and walks on foot beside him to a roadside inn. There he spends the rest of the night nursing and watching over him.

The next morning, the Samaritan gives two silver coins to the innkeeper, which would pay for several days of lodging and meals. He promises to return and pay for any extra expenses needed to nurse the traveler back to health. He makes sure the hurt man is completely cared for without asking for anything back.

Jesus ends the story by asking the lawyer which of the three travelers acted like a true neighbor. This turns the lawyer's original question completely around. Instead of debating who deserves to receive our love, Jesus shows that we should freely give mercy to anyone who is in need.

The lawyer cannot bear to say the word Samaritan, but he admits that the one who showed mercy was the real neighbor. Jesus tells him to go and live the exact same way. True love crosses racial and social lines to bring practical help to people who are hurting.

As Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, He stops in the village of Bethany and is welcomed into the home of a woman named Martha. Martha serves as the head of her household and generously opens her doors to host Jesus and His followers. Her hospitality shows genuine respect and affection for the Lord.

Martha's sister Mary sits on the floor at the feet of Jesus, listening closely to everything He teaches. In Bible times, sitting at a teacher's feet was the regular posture of a humble student. Mary eagerly takes this rare opportunity to receive spiritual nourishment directly from Christ.

Martha feels overwhelmed and pulled in different directions by all the work needed to prepare the meal. Frustrated and exhausted, she interrupts Jesus and asks Him to command Mary to help her. In her stress, Martha's good desire to serve has turned into anger toward her sister and irritation with the Lord.

Jesus repeats Martha's name twice with warm, tender concern. He does not scold her for serving food, but He points out that her mind has become troubled and divided by too many tasks. Her excessive worry over household details was robbing her of inner peace.

Jesus explains that only one thing is truly necessary, and Mary made the better choice by sitting to hear His word. Physical food will soon disappear, but the eternal truth and grace Mary receives can never be taken away. While serving others is important, resting in Christ and listening to Him must always come first.

differ.view: Presbyterians and Reformed teachers emphasize that Jesus was not calling Martha's serving bad, but comparing good work with the even greater duty of feeding upon Christ's word.
Lutherans see the sisters as reflecting the twin callings of loving neighbor and loving God, viewing Martha's distress as a natural human limit rather than bad intent.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest that Martha and Mary were each involved in recognized forms of early Christian leadership, with Martha serving as an active church host and minister rather than just a busy cook.
